structured_output.hypothesis: If the claim holds, in a large census of species the gametic (haploid) chromosome number n falls mostly between 6 and 16, with species at n<6 uncommon and species at n>16 rarer still.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using one n value per species (the species median of its recorded gametic n values), all three of the following hold: (a) at least 75% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; (b) at most 15% of species have n < 6; (c) the share of species with n > 16 is smaller than the share with n < 6.
structured_output.fail_criterion: Any one of the following: fewer than 60% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; more than 25% of species have n < 6; or the share with n > 16 is greater than or equal to the share with n < 6. Results between the pass and fail thresholds are inconclusive and reported as such.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'germ-nuclei' are the gametic nuclei, so the test uses the haploid number n, not the somatic 2n. 'Few' is read as at most 15% and 'mostly' as at least 75%. 'Fewer still more than sixteen' is read as a strictly smaller share above 16 than below 6. Modern knowledge adds polyploidy, which was not understood in 1917 and may push many plant counts above 16. Records given only as 2n are halved to n, and records of mixed ploidy are not corrected. The Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB) covers plants only (Rice et al. 2015), so this test covers the plant half of the claim's scope ('plants and animals'). It cannot decide the animal half, and a pass or fail must not be extended to animals. I did not verify the current URL or a DOI, so the DOI is null.

dataset.name: Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB)
dataset.publisher: Tel Aviv University (Rice et al., Chromosome Counts Database; New Phytologist 2015)
dataset.why_it_fits: CCDB aggregates published chromosome counts for tens of thousands of plant taxa. Fields to use: taxon (species name), gametic number n, sporophytic number 2n, and the record's source reference. Counts are collapsed to one n per species and binned as <6, 6-16 and >16 to compute the pass and fail quantities.
